advisor_letter:
Dear [[CLIENT_NAME]],

You are ten years from the retirement age you have set for yourself, and you are in the phase where the decisions made now compound the most. At fifty, with a corporation still active and a sale planned for the same year you intend to step back, the choices about how value leaves that company would shape the next forty years more than almost anything else you could do. That is precisely why this report exists: to look honestly at where the projection lands today.

The work that brought you here is real. You have built roughly $345K across registered, tax-free, and non-registered accounts, and your corporation carries substantial retained earnings alongside an operating business. Your retirement income would lean heavily on QPP/CPP and OAS, with personal savings layered on top — and the single structural choice that already defines this file is how the corporation's value is extracted and integrated as you transition out.

This report is built to deliver answers, not just topics. The executive summary gives you the verdict in thirty seconds. Chapter I sets out the foundations and the projection. Chapter II describes the risk you would be taking under different futures. Chapter III walks through the strategies and decisions in front of you. Chapter IV offers alternatives you could test. I encourage particular attention to Chapter III, because the order in which corporate value is drawn is where this file's outcome would move the most.

With respect for the work ahead,
Your BuildFi analyst

Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any observation in this report.
overall_assessment: Across 5000 simulated futures, the plan reaches a **26%** success rate, a grade of F that places this file in rebuilding territory rather than a fragile-but-passing zone. The single greatest structural strength is the corporation — **850K$** in retained earnings plus an operating business sold at age 60 — whose extraction order (salary versus dividend, and how the proceeds integrate with personal and public income) would influence the result more than any other lever. The single greatest risk is the gap between planned spending and durable income: the projection shows savings depleted at age 71, well inside the forty-year horizon. One actionable observation: because guaranteed income covers only **30%** of the target, the sequencing of corporate distributions ahead of the sale is where the plan's trajectory would shift most. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on these observations.
verdict: The dispersion here is narrow for an unsettling reason: median (P50) real wealth lands at **0$** and even the cautious P25 scenario sits at **0$**, with only the favourable P75 path reaching **39K$**. When three of the four reference points cluster at zero, the spread is tight not because outcomes are certain in a good sense, but because most simulated futures exhaust personal capital before the horizon closes. The plan would benefit from material adjustments rather than fine-tuning.
page_zero_verdict: You appear to be carrying the quiet weight of a business owner approaching an exit — wanting the company you built to translate cleanly into a retirement that holds, without surprises in the decade that matters most. That concern is well placed, and this report is written around it.
profile_summary: Your personal capital totals roughly **345K$**, split across a **180K$** RRSP, a **95K$** TFSA, and **70K$** in non-registered holdings — a diversified three-account structure that gives flexibility on withdrawal ordering. The allocation sits at 66.7% equity and 33.3% bonds, a growth-tilted mix consistent with a ten-year accumulation runway. The notable feature is that personal savings are modest relative to the **850K$** held inside the corporation, so the file's centre of gravity is corporate rather than personal.
trajectory_insight: The projected real wealth path crosses zero in most futures: median (P50) and cautious (P25) endpoints both land at **0$**, while the favourable (P75) scenario preserves only **39K$**. The spread is driven less by market dispersion than by the structural mismatch between a 7.4% initial withdrawal rate and the income the portfolio can sustain. In plain terms, the trajectory bends toward depletion well before the projected horizon under most of the 5000 simulated futures.
income_insight: Guaranteed income coverage reaches **30%** of the retirement target, with QPP/CPP as the dominant source at **$1,623** monthly alongside **$1,193** in OAS, for **$3,859** in combined public income. Against monthly spending of **$7,500**, that leaves a gap of **$9,049** that personal and corporate capital would need to fill. The structural reading is that public benefits form the backbone of the income floor, with extracted corporate value and personal savings layered on as the complement that closes the gap.
taxInsight: The average effective tax rate across the projection sits at **16.3%**, modest relative to gross income and consistent with a profile drawing meaningfully on public benefits and lower-bracket withdrawals. Lifetime tax totals **275K$** in real terms, and the model records **0** years of OAS clawback, so no recovery tax erodes the OAS stream in this scenario. The dominant lever is the order in which corporate value is extracted — salary versus dividend, and how CCPC integration interacts with personal RRSP and TFSA draws — since that sequencing shapes both the effective rate and the durability of after-tax income. Tax-savings figures versus a naive strategy are not available in this projection, so none is quoted. As an Ontario file, bracket thresholds differ from Quebec, which would alter the relative cost of dividend versus salary extraction compared with a QC-resident plan.
estateInsight: The projected net estate is **0$**, with **0$** in tax at death, which is a direct consequence of savings being depleted at age 71 rather than a planning outcome in itself. With no residual capital projected in the median path, there is no meaningful estate transfer to analyze in this scenario. The estate picture would change materially only if the income gap were narrowed enough to leave capital intact through the horizon.
gis_insight: The model projects **23** years of GIS eligibility and **388K$** in lifetime GIS, averaging **$16,876** per year, which reflects the low taxable-income profile that emerges once personal savings are drawn down. Eligibility of this kind sits against the well-known threshold dynamic, where each additional dollar of certain income can reduce GIS by roughly fifty cents — the 50¢ clawback that makes the order and timing of corporate and registered withdrawals consequential. GIS appears here as part of the public income floor at certain income levels, not as a destination the plan should aim for.
corp_insight: The corporation holds **850K$** in retained earnings against **250K$** in annual revenue, with a sale planned at age 60 — making it the structural centre of this file. The order in which that value is extracted — salary to create RRSP room and CPP contributions, dividends to integrate with the personal bracket, and the treatment of sale proceeds — would shape after-tax income and durability more than any personal-account decision. Because CCPC integration interacts directly with the modest personal capital and the public income floor, the extraction sequence is the lever where this plan's outcome would move the most.
riskInsight: The dispersion between the cautious P25 endpoint at **0$** and the favourable P75 at **39K$** is compressed because depletion dominates most paths, with savings durability showing depletion at age 71. The driver of this spread is primarily spending variance against a thin income floor: the **$9,049** monthly gap leaves little tolerance for adverse sequence-of-returns near the retirement date. Among the modelled factors, the sensitivity to spending and withdrawal pace matters most, since returns and inflation swings both leave the median endpoint at zero.
stress_interpretation: Under stress, the plan is most vulnerable to stagflation, where the success rate falls to 6% (a sharp Δ below the 26% baseline), with persistent inflation and a lost decade close behind at 13% each. It holds up comparatively best under the longevity-plus-five scenario at 20% and the 2008-style shock at 18%, but no scenario reaches a comfortable zone — the pattern indicates a plan strained at its foundation rather than exposed to a single isolated shock. Because the projection sits at F, a recovery trajectory matters more than a diagnosis, and the elements within your control could be sequenced as follows: first, stabilize the spending target, since the **$9,049** monthly gap is the largest single pressure on durability; then, sequence the corporate extraction ahead of the age-60 sale so that the **850K$** in retained earnings integrates as favourably as possible with personal and public income; next, rebuild the personal capital runway across the **180K$** RRSP, **95K$** TFSA, and **70K$** non-registered accounts during the ten remaining accumulation years; and finally, re-plan the retirement-age and income targets once the corporate transition is structured. Consult a certified financial planner before acting on any of these observations.
